metadata.title: Checkout drop-off triage
metadata.description: A mid-funnel drop-off on a mobile checkout: frame the problem, investigate the evidence, decide what to learn next, then validate your call.

initialProblem.statement: Mobile checkout completion fell 6 points quarter over quarter while traffic stayed flat.

historicalContext.change: Shipping-cost estimator added to the cart screen
Apple Pay enabled for returning customers only

evidence.supportTickets: 12 tickets mention 'no Apple Pay at payment step'

rootCause.primary: Payment-step friction for iOS customers who see Apple Pay in the cart and lose it at payment
rootCause.alternative: Shipping estimator pushes cart-to-checkout dwell time up on slow connections

opportunity.statement: Make the payment step match the promise the cart screen makes.

solutionDirections.direction: Offer every iOS customer the same payment methods end to end
Defer the shipping estimator until after the address step

validation.cheapestTest: Replay the payment step in a moderated 5-person tap-through of the iOS flow
validation.metric: checkoutStart to purchase conversion on iOS

applicantSteps.context: Mobile checkout completion dropped 6 points quarter over quarter while traffic held flat. Growth wants a cause, not a redesign.
applicantSteps.question: Before digging in, which framing of the problem is most useful?

options.text: Checkout is too long; shorten the flow and remove steps.
Define the drop as a conversion question on a specific step and segment, then find what changed.
Users are abandoning because shipping costs feel high; add a free-shipping banner.
The funnel numbers are noisy; ask engineering to double-check the analytics pipeline first.

applicantSteps.context: You have two weeks, one designer and one analyst. Support has 12 tickets mentioning Apple Pay.

rows.note: Apple Pay enabled for returning customers only

applicantSteps.question: What is the most informative next move?

options.text: Ship the 12 support tickets to the growth channel as the diagnosis and start on a payment-method redesign.
Isolate the iOS payment step, compare it to the Android flow at the same step, and trace what changed in that screen.
Build a full checkout redesign prototype and test it against the current flow.
Run a survey asking all users why they abandoned checkout.

applicantSteps.context: The payment-step drop is concentrated on iOS, where Apple Pay is offered only to returning customers, yet the cart screen advertises it to everyone.
applicantSteps.question: Write the single riskiest assumption behind a fix for this drop, and say how you would prove it wrong this week.

applicantSteps.context: You have a hypothesis: iOS customers who see Apple Pay in the cart and lose it at payment abandon at that step.
applicantSteps.question: Which evidence would actually challenge that hypothesis?

options.text: Session replays of iOS customers who reached the payment step without Apple Pay, checking for backtracking or repeated taps.
A new dashboard showing that payment-step conversion is, in fact, down.
A survey of users who already purchased asking whether they like the checkouts they completed.
An internal review confirming that the Apple Pay rule is intentional.

answerSheet.objective: Frame the drop as a measurable, segmentable problem before proposing solutions.

A.reasoningSignal: Jumps to a solution without locating the drop or its segment.
A.consequence: Work starts on a redesign of a flow that may not be the problem.
reveal: The funnel shows the largest relative loss between checkout start and payment step.

B.reasoningSignal: Localises the problem to a step and a segment before spending effort.
B.consequence: You get a comparable slice of the funnel and can ask what changed.
reveal: Splitting by platform shows the drop is concentrated on iOS.

C.reasoningSignal: Asserts a cause from a hypothesis the data has not yet supported.
C.consequence: A banner ships, the metric may move for unrelated reasons, and the cause stays unknown.
reveal: Shipping cost appears in only 3 of the 12 support tickets.

D.reasoningSignal: Treats a measurable, stable funnel as instrument error.
D.consequence: Two weeks can be spent validating analytics rather than the product change.
reveal: The analytics pipeline change was four months ago; the drop is six weeks old.

answerSheet.objective: Compare like with like and look for a specific change, rather than collecting more opinion.

A.reasoningSignal: Treats support tickets as a diagnosis and moves straight to a fix.
A.consequence: The redesign ships without evidence, and the same step may still lose customers.
reveal: 12 tickets are suggestive, but they are 0.05% of the affected iOS traffic.

B.reasoningSignal: Controls the comparison and traces the specific screen change on the affected segment.
B.consequence: You connect a dated change (Apple Pay for returning customers only) to the step where the loss appears.
reveal: The cart screen advertises Apple Pay to all iOS users; the payment step offers it only to returning customers.

C.reasoningSignal: Scopes a redesign before the cause is known.
C.consequence: Effort goes into a prototype that cannot confirm the mechanism.
reveal: A prototype would test a solution, not the cause of the drop.

D.reasoningSignal: Collects stated preference instead of observing behaviour.
D.consequence: You learn what people say about checkout, not what happened at the payment step.
reveal: Stated reasons rarely match the step where behaviour actually stops.

answerSheet.objective: State a falsifiable assumption and a cheap test that could disprove it.

A.reasoningSignal: Names an assumption that is specific, checkable, and tied to the observed segment.
A.consequence: A five-person replay either shows the loss moment or kills the hypothesis cheaply.
reveal: Payment-step replays are the cheapest evidence that can disconfirm the mechanism.

B.reasoningSignal: Restates the problem without an assumption that could be wrong.
B.consequence: No test can fail, so the team learns nothing either way.
reveal: An assumption that cannot be falsified cannot be validated.

answerSheet.objective: Choose evidence that can disconfirm the hypothesis rather than confirm it.

A.reasoningSignal: Looks for the moment of failure in the affected segment - evidence that could refute the hypothesis.
A.consequence: Either the replays show the loss at payment, or the hypothesis dies before any build.
reveal: Replays show repeated taps on the payment step for customers who saw Apple Pay in the cart.
Recommended fix: offer the same payment methods from cart through payment for iOS customers.

B.reasoningSignal: Re-measures the symptom instead of testing the mechanism.
B.consequence: You confirm the drop again and still cannot explain it.
reveal: The funnel already showed the drop; this adds no new information.

C.reasoningSignal: Asks successful customers about a flow they never abandoned.
C.consequence: Survivorship bias leaves the cause untested.
reveal: Purchasers are the one group that did not experience the drop.

D.reasoningSignal: Substitutes the team's intent for the customer's experience.
D.consequence: An intentional rule can still be a broken experience; the drop stays unexplained.
reveal: Intent explains why the rule exists, not why the drop happens.
